title: Your map of suffering
hook: which teachings and practices actually help you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seneca's letter about a city burned in one night. Your line was it can rise. What first stone did you set? Today, we start to close the question of suffering, with a pencil. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

An old trail map, folded and refolded until the creases have gone soft. Someone has written on it in pencil. A circle around a spring: good water. An X on a shortcut: don't, it floods. A star on a ledge: sat here, saw everything. The printed map shows the whole mountain. The pencil shows what one walker learned on it. For weeks now this path has been walking through suffering, with teachings from many traditions. Today, the pencil comes out.
screen: `A MAP WITH PENCIL MARKS.` → `GOOD WATER. DON'T, IT FLOODS.` → `TODAY, THE PENCIL COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: First, a map, not a creed. A creed says what is true for everyone. A map of suffering says something smaller and more useful: what has actually helped this one person, on this one road. It doesn't have to settle why suffering exists. It only has to mark the springs and the floods. Second, look back at what we've walked. The Buddha's teaching of the second arrow: the pain, and then the pain we add to it. The psalmist's question, how long, said straight to God. Patience, sabr, in the Qur'an. The friends who sat with Job in silence, before they ruined it by talking. Viktor Frankl's last freedom, the choice of an attitude. These last two weeks: a small mercy, a quiet hour, one day at a time, a city rising. Each came from its own tradition, and each stays with its own source. Your map can hold several without blending them into one teaching. Third, two columns. On one side, what helps. On the other, what doesn't, even when it's supposed to. Some people find advice makes things worse, and silence helps. Some find a practice that works on a bad day and fails on a terrible one. Both are worth writing down. An honest map has X marks too. Fourth, maps change. A map drawn young looks different later on. A teaching that meant nothing last year may be the spring you need next year. So the map stays in pencil. Write it today, and expect to erase.
screen: `A MAP, NOT A CREED.` · `WHAT WE'VE WALKED, EACH IN ITS PLACE.` · `WHAT HELPS, WHAT DOESN'T.` · `KEEP IT IN PENCIL.` · then, large: `WHAT HELPS ME.`

segments.voice: Take a piece of paper, or a note on your phone. Draw a line down the middle. On the left, write what helps when things are hard: a teaching, a practice, a person, a place, a song. On the right, what doesn't help, even if it's meant to. Don't think too long. Three on each side is plenty. Then sit quietly and look at the left column. Notice which one you'd reach for first. If you pray, prayer may be on your map; it belongs there if it helps. The bell holds the time.
Your map of suffering: a pencil map, in two columns, of the teachings and practices that actually help you, each kept with its source. Today's word.
Your line: what helps me. Today, keep the map somewhere you'll find it on a bad day, and add one mark before bed. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some people keep a written list of what helps in hard times, from scripture verses and prayers to walks and phone numbers, and some therapists and chaplains help people draw up such a plan before a crisis.

fork.setup: a friend's advice, meant kindly, always makes your bad days worse. where does it go on the map?
options: leave it off; it was meant well.
fork.reveal: an honest map has X marks too. writing it down isn't unkind; it's knowing the terrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: you need the one right answer to suffering before anything can help.
what it means: a personal pencil map of what actually helps, with many sources kept apart.
what a scholar hears: a closing review of the block: the second arrow (Sallatha Sutta), Psalm 13, sabr, Job 2:13, Frankl's 'last of the human freedoms'.
